strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: making pixel-space diffusion transformers competitive without relying on a pretrained autoencoder. The motivation is clear, especially for fine-detail preservation and avoiding VAE reconstruction artifacts.

The proposed dual-level design is technically sensible: a coarse patch-level DiT handles global semantics while a lightweight pixel-level transformer performs local refinement. Pixel-wise AdaLN and pixel token compaction are well described and directly address the main computational obstacle of dense pixel attention.

The ImageNet evidence is strong for the central claim. PixelDiT-XL reports 1.61 gFID at 320 epochs, outperforming several recent pixel-space models such as PixelFlow, PixNerd, EPG, and JiT-G under the reported comparison, with competitive recall and reasonable compute.

The ablation section is useful. The progression from vanilla DiT/16 to RoPE/RMSNorm, token compaction, and pixel-wise AdaLN supports the claim that the pixel-level pathway and conditioning mechanism matter. The compute ablation also shows why uncompacted pixel attention is impractical.

The paper demonstrates scalability beyond class-conditional ImageNet through text-to-image results at 512 and 1024 resolution, where PixelDiT-T2I achieves strong GenEval and DPG-Bench numbers relative to both pixel-space and several latent diffusion baselines.

The manuscript is generally clear and contains many implementation details, including architecture sizes, optimizer settings, guidance intervals, sampler choices, and additional category-wise benchmark breakdowns.
weaknesses: The text-to-image training data is insufficiently specified: the paper only states that approximately 26M image-text pairs were collected. Without dataset composition, filtering, deduplication, licensing, or overlap analysis with GenEval/DPG-Bench prompts/images, the T2I results are hard to interpret and reproduce.

Reproducibility remains limited despite hyperparameter tables. There is no indication of code, pretrained weights, exact data preprocessing, compute budget, or random seed sensitivity. The 1024-resolution T2I model in particular would be difficult for others to verify.

The comparison to latent diffusion models is somewhat uneven. The paper emphasizes avoiding autoencoders, but the strongest latent baselines still have better ImageNet FID, and throughput/compute comparisons do not fully account for differences in sampling steps, implementation, hardware, model release status, or end-to-end system costs.

The image editing claim is under-supported. The paper presents a compelling qualitative example where PixelDiT preserves wall text better than SD3/FLUX reconstructions, but this is essentially anecdotal; there is no quantitative editing benchmark, no broader set of examples in the main evaluation, and no analysis of cases where pixel-space editing may fail.

The method still uses external pretrained representation supervision through frozen DINOv2 for REPA-style alignment. This is not an autoencoder, but it weakens the cleanest interpretation of fully end-to-end pixel-space training and deserves more explicit discussion and ablation, especially for the headline ImageNet results.

Several design choices are validated only on ImageNet 256. There is little ablation for the text-to-image setting, including whether pixel-wise AdaLN, compaction rate, REPA, text routing only through patch tokens, and the chosen patch/pixel depths remain optimal at 1024 resolution.

The novelty is meaningful but somewhat architectural/integration-based: patch-level semantic modeling, compacted local-to-global processing, AdaLN conditioning, MM-DiT, rectified flow, and REPA are all close to existing ingredients. The paper would benefit from sharper positioning against related hierarchical or decoupled transformer designs.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants, such as saying compaction does not compromise fine details because residual connections preserve high-frequency information. The ablations support good FID, but they do not directly measure high-frequency preservation except through qualitative examples.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely question: whether transformer diffusion can be made practical directly in pixel space without a VAE/autoencoder bottleneck. This is a meaningful direction for image fidelity and editing applications.

The proposed dual-level design is plausible and reasonably motivated: coarse patch-level DiT blocks handle global semantics, while a lightweight pixel pathway with pixel-wise AdaLN and token compaction attempts to restore local detail efficiently.

The ImageNet 256x256 results are strong among reported pixel-space generative models: PixelDiT-XL reports gFID 1.61 with 797M parameters, improving over PixelFlow, PixNerd, EPG, and JiT in the main comparison.

The paper includes useful ablations on core components, patch size, model size, solver choice, guidance settings, depth allocation, and token compaction. These experiments support the claim that the pixel pathway and pixel-wise modulation matter.
The manuscript is mostly clear, with enough architectural detail to understand the method at a high level. The appendix adds helpful implementation settings for ImageNet and text-to-image training.
weaknesses: The central novelty is less clean than advertised. The model still compresses each p x p pixel block to a compact token before global attention, so the distinction from strong patch-token DiTs is partly architectural degree rather than a fundamentally new pixel modeling paradigm. The paper repeatedly frames this as dense per-pixel modeling, but the global interaction still happens after aggressive compaction.

The strongest text-to-image claims are hard to assess scientifically because the 26M image-text training set is only vaguely described. Data source, filtering, caption quality, licensing, duplicates, and overlap with evaluation prompts are not specified, making reproducibility and fairness difficult to judge.

The text-to-image comparisons are not fully controlled. The paper compares against large public systems such as SDXL, DALLE 3, FLUX, Hunyuan-DiT, and PixArt with different data, training regimes, safety filters, samplers, guidance, and possible prompt processing. The resulting GenEval/DPG numbers are useful but do not by themselves establish architectural superiority.

The image editing claim is weakly supported. Figure 1(b) is an anecdotal qualitative example, and no quantitative editing benchmark, user study, or broader sample set is provided. The conclusion that PixelDiT significantly improves editing detail preservation is therefore under-evidenced.

The paper underplays some competing evidence. It notes that SiD2 reports lower gFID than PixelDiT but excludes it from the main table due to missing metadata; this is reasonable for fairness, but the paper still uses strong language about outperforming pixel models that should be qualified more carefully.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives hyperparameters, but does not indicate code/model release, training compute budget, hardware scale, wall-clock cost, or precise construction of the T2I dataset. For a large-scale generative model paper, these omissions materially limit independent verification.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially phrases such as a breakthrough at 1024 pixel-space T2I and claims that compaction does not compromise fine-grained details. The experiments show good benchmark scores, but do not directly isolate high-frequency preservation across diverse scenarios.

The ImageNet gains, while strong, require a large 797M-parameter model, extensive tuning of guidance/sampler settings, representation alignment with a frozen DINOv2 encoder, and 1.6M training iterations. The paper would be stronger with a clearer accounting of total compute and controlled comparisons under matched training budgets.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely question: whether DiT-style generative modeling can be made practical directly in pixel space, avoiding the reconstruction bottleneck of latent autoencoders. The framing is clear and relevant to both image generation and editing.

The proposed architecture is technically plausible and well motivated. The separation between a patch-level semantic pathway and a lightweight pixel-level pathway, together with pixel-wise AdaLN and pixel token compaction, directly addresses the compute bottleneck of dense pixel attention.

The ImageNet 256x256 results are strong for pixel-space generation. PixelDiT-XL reports 1.61 gFID at 320 epochs, improving over several recent pixel-space baselines such as PixelFlow-XL, PixNerd-XL, EPG, and JiT-G, while using a forward-pass compute closer to latent DiT models than many prior pixel models.

The ablations are useful and mostly convincing. Table 4 shows large gains from the dual-level design plus compaction and pixel-wise AdaLN, Table 5 isolates the role of pixel-pathway attention, and the appendix studies patch size, depth allocation, solver choice, CFG settings, and compaction rate.

The extension to text-to-image generation is a meaningful demonstration of scalability. The reported GenEval and DPG-Bench scores at 512 and 1024 resolution are competitive, especially for a pixel-space model, and the throughput comparison suggests the design is not merely high quality but also practically efficient.
The manuscript is generally clear, with sufficient architectural details, training hyperparameters, and appendix material to understand the method and reproduce the main ImageNet setup in principle.
weaknesses: The text-to-image evidence is less reproducible and harder to interpret because the 26M image-text training set is private or insufficiently specified. Since the T2I claims are a major part of the paper, more detail on data source, filtering, licensing, captioning, and possible overlap with evaluation prompts would be needed for a fully convincing comparison.

The editing claim is supported mainly by a single qualitative FlowEdit example. The argument that pixel-space modeling preserves details better than VAE-based latent models is plausible, but the paper does not provide a systematic editing benchmark, multiple seeds/prompts, or quantitative preservation metrics, so this part remains anecdotal.

Some comparisons mix models trained with different data, objectives, parameter counts, training budgets, samplers, and guidance tuning. The paper is transparent about many settings, but the headline tables still make it difficult to isolate how much of the gain comes from the architecture versus training recipe, solver/CFG choices, REPA alignment, or scale.

The novelty is incremental in some components: the work combines known ingredients such as DiT backbones, RMSNorm/RoPE, REPA-style alignment, MM-DiT text conditioning, and rectified-flow sampling. The main architectural contribution is the dual-level pixel/patch organization with pixel-wise modulation and compaction; this is valuable, but the paper could better distinguish it from related hierarchical or patchified pixel models.

The claim that token compaction does not compromise fine details is stronger than the evidence supports. The mechanism still compresses local pixel tokens before attention, and the paper relies on residual paths and empirical FID rather than direct analyses of high-frequency fidelity, reconstruction limits, or failure cases caused by compaction.

Although the ImageNet results are strong among pixel-space models, the method still trails the best latent-space models in FID and depends on a large 797M-parameter model and long training. The paper makes a good case for pixel-space feasibility, but not yet for replacing latent models broadly.

Reproducibility would be stronger with released code, exact FLOP-counting scripts, training compute budget, data preprocessing details, and random-seed variability. The reported results appear credible, but large-scale generative results can be sensitive to these details.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely question: whether transformer diffusion models can be made competitive directly in pixel space, avoiding VAE reconstruction artifacts. The proposed dual-level design is well motivated: a patch-level DiT handles global semantics while a lightweight pixel-level pathway handles local refinement.

The empirical results are strong for the stated goal. PixelDiT-XL reports 1.61 gFID on ImageNet 256 and 1.81 gFID on ImageNet 512, improving over most listed pixel-space generative models, and the text-to-image variant reports competitive GenEval/DPG scores at both 512 and 1024 resolution.

The ablation coverage is better than typical: the manuscript studies pixel token compaction, pixel-wise AdaLN, patch size, model scale, depth allocation, sampler choice, guidance settings, REPA, compaction rate, ImageNet-512 patch size, compute estimates, extended training, and even negative attempts. This gives meaningful support to the architectural claims.

The efficiency story is plausible and quantitatively supported. The reported 311 GFLOPs at ImageNet 256 is close to latent DiT-style models and far below several pixel-space alternatives, while maintaining a strong FID.

The editing experiment, though narrow, highlights a real practical advantage of pixel-space models: avoiding VAE reconstruction damage in unedited regions. The appendix quantifies this on 281 FlowEdit samples using background MSE/SSIM.

The paper is generally clear and reproducible at the architecture/training-recipe level, with model sizes, depths, dimensions, optimizer settings, guidance intervals, sampling steps, and many evaluation settings specified.
weaknesses: A central framing issue is that the method is described as end-to-end pixel-space training without auxiliary bottlenecks, but the reported ImageNet performance depends heavily on REPA alignment to a frozen DINOv2 encoder. The ablation shows performance degrades severely without REPA, so the contribution is not as independent of pretrained representation machinery as the main narrative suggests.

The novelty is incremental rather than conceptual: the method combines known ingredients such as DiT/MM-DiT blocks, AdaLN-style conditioning, RoPE/RMSNorm, representation alignment, rectified flow, and token compression. The paper’s main value is in the effective system design and scaling evidence, not in a fundamentally new modeling principle.

The text-to-image evaluation uses a 26M image-text dataset described only at a high level. Dataset composition, filtering, licensing, caption source/quality, and possible overlap with evaluation distributions are not detailed, limiting reproducibility and making comparisons with public systems harder to interpret.

Several comparisons are imperfectly controlled. Baselines differ in model size, training budget, data, sampler, guidance, and in some cases missing metrics. The authors acknowledge one strong SiD2 result is excluded from the main table due to missing metadata, but this still complicates the claim of best pixel-space performance.

The editing evidence is suggestive but limited. It compares only against SD3 and FLUX under FlowEdit, focuses on background preservation outside SAM-derived boxes, and does not report edit success, perceptual quality, or human preference, so the editing advantage should be viewed as a preliminary demonstration rather than a complete validation.

The method remains expensive: the main ImageNet model is 797M parameters, extended training reaches 800 epochs, and the T2I model is 1.3B parameters trained at large batch sizes. The paper would benefit from stronger discussion of practical training cost and accessibility.

Some claims around preserving high-frequency details through token compaction are stronger than the direct evidence. The FID/IS ablations support quality, but there is limited targeted analysis of texture fidelity, reconstruction-free detail preservation, or failure modes beyond selected qualitative examples and the editing metric.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely question: whether diffusion transformers can be made practical directly in pixel space without an image autoencoder. The proposed dual-level architecture is clear at a high level and addresses a real computational bottleneck in pixel-space attention.

The ImageNet results are strong among reported pixel-space generative models: PixelDiT-XL reports 1.61 gFID at 256x256 and 1.81 gFID at 512x512, with extensive comparisons to both pixel-space and latent-space models.

The ablations are useful and identify several influential components. In particular, the comparisons for token compaction, pixel-wise AdaLN, REPA, patch size, solver choice, guidance settings, and depth allocation help explain the design choices.

The appendix provides unusually many implementation details, including model sizes, optimization settings, sampling steps, guidance intervals, FLOP estimates, and negative results, which improves the paper's practical value.
The text-to-image extension is ambitious, and the reported GenEval/DPG-Bench numbers suggest that pixel-space DiTs can be competitive beyond class-conditioned ImageNet generation.
weaknesses: The central novelty is less convincing than the presentation suggests. Compressing pixels within a patch to a compact token for global attention, then expanding back with residual/local modulation, is close in spirit to patch-token DiTs with a learned local decoder/refinement pathway. The paper should more clearly distinguish this from existing hierarchical, patchified, and local-refinement transformer designs.

Several major claims are overstated. The manuscript repeatedly states that pixel token compaction does not compromise fine detail because residual paths preserve high-frequency information, but this is asserted rather than directly tested. A learned p^2-token-to-one-token projection is still a bottleneck inside each block, and the evidence does not isolate whether fine detail is truly preserved by the proposed mechanism.

The strongest performance depends heavily on external representation alignment with a frozen DINOv2 encoder. Table 11 shows a large degradation without REPA, so the method is not just a self-contained pixel-space diffusion architecture. This dependency weakens the claim that the proposed pixel modeling alone makes the approach practical and creates a confound in the ablations.

The text-to-image evaluation is difficult to reproduce. The model is trained on an unspecified 26M image-text dataset at high resolution, with a frozen Gemma-2 text encoder and substantial compute. Dataset composition, filtering, licensing, and training cost are not described enough to assess fairness or reproducibility.

Comparisons are not always fully controlled. The ImageNet results use different training lengths, guidance settings, solvers, parameter counts, and auxiliary losses across methods, while some baselines rely on reported numbers from papers. This is acceptable as a broad benchmark table, but it limits the strength of claims about superiority and efficiency.

The editing claim is under-supported relative to its prominence. Figure 1 shows a compelling example and Table 14 reports background MSE/SSIM on 281 FlowEdit samples, but there is little analysis of edit success, prompt fidelity, failure modes, or whether the comparison is controlled for model capacity and editing hyperparameters.

The method is expensive despite the efficiency framing. PixelDiT-XL has 797M parameters, uses 100 sampling steps for ImageNet, and the 512x512 result requires long fine-tuning. The paper reports FLOPs, but wall-clock training cost, memory usage, and end-to-end sampling latency including all conditioning components are not sufficiently characterized.

The paper's clarity is generally good, but it occasionally blurs terminology. Calling the system single-stage and end-to-end is potentially misleading when training relies on frozen DINOv2 features and T2I relies on a frozen text encoder; it is more accurate to say it avoids a pretrained image autoencoder.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: whether diffusion transformers can be made practical directly in pixel space, avoiding the autoencoder bottleneck of latent diffusion. This is a meaningful contribution for image generation and editing, not just an incremental benchmark tweak.

The proposed dual-level architecture is technically well motivated. Separating coarse patch-level semantic modeling from pixel-level refinement, and using pixel-wise AdaLN plus pixel token compaction, gives a clear mechanism for reducing the cost of dense pixel modeling while retaining fine detail.

The empirical results are strong for pixel-space generation. PixelDiT-XL reports 1.61 FID on ImageNet 256 and 1.81 FID on ImageNet 512, outperforming several recent pixel-space baselines, with competitive compute relative to other pixel methods.

The ablation section is unusually helpful. The paper isolates RoPE/RMSNorm, token compaction, pixel-wise AdaLN, patch size, model scale, pixel-pathway attention, REPA, solver choice, guidance settings, and compaction rate. These experiments support the central architectural claims.

The text-to-image extension is a valuable demonstration of scalability. The reported GenEval/DPG scores at 512 and 1024 resolution are competitive with much larger latent diffusion systems and stronger than prior pixel-space baselines in the tables.

The editing discussion highlights a practical advantage of pixel-space models: avoiding VAE reconstruction artifacts. The qualitative example and background-consistency evaluation on 281 FlowEdit samples support the claim that unedited regions can be preserved better than with latent-space models.
weaknesses: The strongest claims about surpassing latent-space approaches should be tempered. On ImageNet, several latent models in the paper’s own tables still achieve better FID than PixelDiT, and the method relies on a large 797M-parameter model, 100-step sampling, REPA supervision from DINOv2, and substantial training. The contribution is strongest as a high-quality pixel-space model, not as a general replacement for latent diffusion.

The comparison budgets are not fully uniform. Baselines differ in training epochs, parameter counts, sampling procedures, guidance settings, preprocessing, and sometimes unavailable metrics. The paper reports useful tables, but the strength of some efficiency and convergence conclusions is limited by these heterogeneous settings.

Reproducibility of the text-to-image result is only partial. The 26M image-text dataset is described at a high level but not sufficiently specified, and the data curation, filtering, licensing, prompt preprocessing, and evaluation implementation details are not enough to reproduce the reported T2I performance independently.

The method is less autoencoder-free than the framing sometimes suggests, in the sense that it depends strongly on representation alignment to a frozen DINOv2 encoder. The REPA ablation shows severe degradation without this auxiliary feature supervision, so the paper should discuss this dependency more directly as part of the recipe rather than a minor add-on.

The image-editing evidence is promising but narrow. The main qualitative comparison focuses on a VAE artifact case, and the quantitative background-preservation metric does not fully measure whether the edited object, prompt compliance, or semantic edit quality are equally good across models.

Training stability remains a material limitation. The authors acknowledge loss spikes and instability for deeper/longer pixel-space training; this matters because the practical recipe appears sensitive to optimizer, clipping, prediction target, timestep sampling, and auxiliary alignment choices.

Some architectural novelty is compositional rather than fundamentally new: dual pathways, AdaLN conditioning, compaction/projection, MM-DiT, rectified flow, and REPA each connect closely to prior work. The originality lies in the integration and empirical validation for pixel-space DiTs, which is solid but not a clean new theoretical advance.
